analysis.one_liner: Bans employers from forcing workers to arbitrate job disputes or sign away class-action rights.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the Senate health and labor committee on the day it was introduced and no action followed before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal to require an employee, as a condition of getting or keeping a job, to sign a contract agreeing to arbitrate future workplace disputes. It would also bar employers from punishing workers who refuse such agreements, require a 45-day cooling-off period with written disclosures before a worker could voluntarily agree to arbitrate a dispute that already happened, and amend labor law to protect workers' right to bring joint or class lawsuits. Millions of workers sign such clauses today, which means claims like unpaid wages or discrimination are decided privately, one worker at a time, rather than in open court.
analysis.who_benefits: The tens of millions of employees covered by forced-arbitration clauses — especially hourly and lower-paid workers with wage, discrimination, or harassment claims. Group lawsuits are often the only affordable way to challenge small-dollar violations, and this bill restores that option and stops retaliation against workers who refuse to sign.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers with wage and discrimination claims

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any pre-dispute agreement requiring arbitration of an employment dispute, so employers can no longer make signing away court access a condition of employment [S2][S3].
Bars employers from retaliating against an employee who refuses to agree to arbitration, and lets a retaliated-against worker sue with attorney's fees [S2][S3].
Protects the right to bring joint, class, or collective lawsuits over employment disputes by adding a new unfair labor practice under the National Labor Relations Act [S2][S3].

Allows arbitration only for disputes that have already arisen, and only if the worker agrees voluntarily, after a 45-day waiting period, with plain-language written disclosure of their rights [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would face the cost of defending claims in court — including the possibility of class actions — instead of resolving them privately through arbitration, where outcomes for individual workers are rarely public and payouts are typically small.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers facing court and class actions

drawbacks.text: Arbitration can be faster and cheaper than court for some individual workers, and critics argue class actions chiefly benefit plaintiffs' lawyers; the bill closes off that forum even for workers who might prefer it (though it leaves voluntary post-dispute arbitration available) [S2][S3].

Employers would face higher litigation costs and class-action exposure, costs that can be passed to consumers or absorbed in hiring — the trade-off supporters accept to make workplace rights enforceable [S2][S3].
The bill applies as of enactment to any dispute arising afterward, even under agreements signed before the law, which would invalidate terms in many existing employment contracts [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades a real cost to employers — more cases litigated in open court, sometimes as class actions — for restoring workers' practical ability to enforce wage, discrimination, and safety rights. Its carve-out for union contracts and its allowance for voluntary, informed post-dispute arbitration show it was drafted to preserve agreed-upon arbitration while ending the take-it-or-leave-it contract clause. The main honest objection is that some workers may prefer arbitration's speed and lower cost; the bill addresses that by allowing it voluntarily after a dispute exists.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, and it sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Patty Murray introduced the bill on November 14, 2018, with 18 Senate cosponsors (17 Democrats and one Independent) [S1][S4][S5].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
No further action — hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — ever occurred, and the 115th Congress ended January 3, 2019 [S1][S5].

The bill was written in direct response to the Supreme Court's 2018 Epic Systems Corp. v. Lewis decision, which held that employers may require employees, as a condition of employment, to waive the right to sue collectively [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that rely on mandatory arbitration clauses keep their ability to resolve workplace claims privately and out of court, and the arbitration industry keeps the stream of cases those clauses feed.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; all 19 original supporters listed were Democrats or an Independent.

against.role: Chairman, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or committee vote; no committee action followed its referral.

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce
against.what_they_did: Opposed legislation to restrict mandatory employment arbitration, arguing it would push routine workplace disputes into costly class litigation.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or Independent; no Senate Republican signed on, and the bill went no further in a Republican-controlled committee and Senate [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Large employers (retail, food service, tech platforms, finance, staffing)
industries.note: These employers use mandatory arbitration clauses to keep wage, discrimination, and harassment claims out of court and to block group lawsuits, where a single small claim is rarely worth litigating. The bill would remove that shield and expose them to class actions, which is why the loss is the public's gain here.

industries.industry: Arbitration providers and defense-side employment law firms
industries.note: Mandatory arbitration clauses create a captive, employer-driven caseload for arbitration firms and for law firms defending claims in private forums. Ending predispute clauses would shrink that market and move disputes into the public court system.

The bill expressly does not apply to arbitration provisions in contracts between employers and labor organizations, preserving union-negotiated grievance arbitration while guaranteeing workers can still enforce statutory rights in court.
